summary.text: For \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\), modular computations in \((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)[\sqrt3]\) show that \(\alpha=2+\sqrt3\) satisfies \(\alpha^{N+1}=1\), while \(\alpha^{(N+1)/q}-1\) is invertible for each prime factor \(q\in\{2,3,100943\}\) of \(N+1\). Thus modulo every prime divisor \(p\mid N\), \(\alpha\) has exact order \(N+1\), forcing \(N+1\le p^2-1\); this contradicts \(p^2\le N\) if \(N\) is composite, so \(N\) is prime and the positive step \(39101\) makes the relevant least step nonzero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 m_0=39101,\qquad M=2\cdot100943\cdot 3^{39101},\qquad
 N=M-1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1.
\]
We will prove that \(N\) is prime. It will then follow immediately that the set of admissible exponents in the definition of \(a(100943)\) is nonempty, since it contains \(39101\).

The primality proof uses arithmetic in a quadratic ring. For every positive integer \(r\), let
\[
 R_r=(\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z)[s]/(s^2-3).
\]
Thus an element of \(R_r\) is represented by a pair \((a,b)\), standing for \(a+bs\), and multiplication is
\[
 (a,b)(c,d)=(ac+3bd,\,ad+bc)\pmod r.
\]
The zero and identity elements are \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\), respectively. Put
\[
 \alpha=(2,1)=2+s\in R_N.
\]

Here is the finite modular certificate used below. All pair operations in this display are performed modulo the exact integer
\(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\):
\[
 \alpha^M=(1,0),                                                    \tag{1}
\]
and each of
\[
 \alpha^{M/2}-(1,0),\qquad
 \alpha^{M/3}-(1,0),\qquad
 \alpha^{M/100943}-(1,0)                                           \tag{2}
\]
is a unit in \(R_N\).

For completeness, these are exact finite modular computations, not probable-prime tests. They can be reproduced as follows. If \(C(a,b)\) denotes the cube of \((a,b)\), then
\[
 C(a,b)=\bigl(a^3+9ab^2,\,3a^2b+3b^3\bigr)\pmod N.                \tag{3}
\]
First compute \(\alpha^{100943}\) by repeated squaring and multiplication. One addition chain used for the exponent is
\[
\begin{aligned}
1,&2,3,6,12,24,48,49,98,196,197,394,788,1576,1577,3154,6308,\\
&12616,12617,25234,25235,50470,50471,100942,100943.
\end{aligned}                                                       \tag{4}
\]
At a doubling one squares the preceding pair, and at each step increasing the exponent by one one multiplies by \(\alpha\). Starting with the resulting pair \(\alpha^{100943}\), iterate the cubing recurrence (3) exactly \(39101\) times. This gives \(\alpha^{100943\cdot3^{39101}}=\alpha^{M/2}\). Starting with \((\alpha^{100943})^2\), iterate (3) \(39100\) times to obtain
\[
 \alpha^{2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39100}}=\alpha^{M/3},
\]
and iterate it \(39101\) times to obtain
\[
 \alpha^{2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}}=\alpha^M=(1,0).
\]
Finally, starting with \(\alpha^2\), iterate (3) \(39101\) times to obtain
\[
 \alpha^{2\cdot3^{39101}}=\alpha^{M/100943}.
\]
These recurrences give (1).

The unit checks in (2) are likewise ordinary Euclidean computations. Explicitly, for each
\(q\in\{2,3,100943\}\), write the pair produced above as
\[
 \alpha^{M/q}=(A_q,B_q)\pmod N
\]
using least nonnegative residues, and set
\[
 D_q=(A_q-1)^2-3B_q^2.
\]
Applying the Euclidean algorithm gives
\[
 \gcd(D_2,N)=\gcd(D_3,N)=\gcd(D_{100943},N)=1.                    \tag{5}
\]
This is exactly the required unit test: if integers \(t_q\) satisfy
\(t_qD_q\equiv1\pmod N\), as supplied by the extended Euclidean algorithm, then
\[
 t_q(A_q-1,-B_q)\cdot(A_q-1,B_q)
   =t_q(D_q,0)=(1,0)\quad\text{in }R_N.
\]
Therefore \(\alpha^{M/q}-1\) has the displayed inverse for each of the three values of \(q\), proving (2). This describes all of the large-number part of the certificate: the addition chain (4), the modular cubing recurrence (3), the endpoint \((1,0)\), and the three Euclidean gcd results (5).

We next prove the general order consequence of this certificate. Let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). Reduction of both coordinates modulo \(p\) gives a ring homomorphism
\[
 R_N\longrightarrow R_p.
\]
Write \(x\) for the image of \(\alpha\) in \(R_p\). Equation (1) gives
\[
 x^M=1.                                                            \tag{6}
\]
Moreover, a unit remains a unit under a ring homomorphism. Consequently, for every
\(q\in\{2,3,100943\}\), the element \(x^{M/q}-1\) is a unit and in particular is nonzero. Hence
\[
 x^{M/2}\ne1,\qquad x^{M/3}\ne1,\qquad
 x^{M/100943}\ne1.                                                \tag{7}
\]
(The zero ring cannot occur here because \(p\) is prime, so \(p>1\).)

We claim that no exponent \(k\) with \(0<k<M\) can satisfy \(x^k=1\). Suppose otherwise, and put
\[
 g=\gcd(M,k).
\]
From \(x^M=x^k=1\), the Euclidean algorithm for the two exponents gives
\[
 x^g=1.                                                            \tag{8}
\]
One way to see this without presupposing that the entire ring is a field is the following. Whenever \(x^a=x^b=1\), division with remainder \(a=tb+r\) gives
\(x^r=x^a(x^b)^{-t}=1\); the inverse of \(x^b=1\) is just \(1\). Iterating the Euclidean algorithm yields (8).

Now \(g\mid M\), and \(g<M\), because \(g\le k<M\). Write \(M=gh\). Then \(h>1\), so some prime \(q\) divides \(h\). The complete prime factorization relevant here is
\[
 M=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}.                                    \tag{9}
\]
The integer \(100943\) is prime; this follows by trial division by the primes at most
\(\sqrt{100943}<318\). Thus every prime divisor of \(M\) is one of
\(2,3,100943\). Therefore the prime \(q\mid h\) belongs to this three-element set. Since
\(h=qc\) for some \(c\), we have
\[
 \frac Mq=gc,
\]
so (8) implies
\[
 x^{M/q}=(x^g)^c=1.
\]
This contradicts the corresponding assertion in (7). This gives all three possible cases explicitly:
if \(q=2\), it contradicts \(x^{M/2}\ne1\); if \(q=3\), it contradicts
\(x^{M/3}\ne1\); and if \(q=100943\), it contradicts
\(x^{M/100943}\ne1\). We have proved
\[
 x^k\ne1\quad(0<k<M).                                             \tag{10}
\]
Together, (6) and (10) say that \(x\) has exact multiplicative order \(M\), in the sense needed below.

It follows that the \(M\) elements
\[
 1,x,x^2,\ldots,x^{M-1}                                           \tag{11}
\]
are pairwise distinct. Indeed, suppose \(0\le i\le j<M\) and
\(x^i=x^j\). Multiplying by \(x^{M-i}\), and using \(x^M=1\), gives
\[
 1=x^{j-i}.
\]
Since \(0\le j-i<M\), (10) forces \(j-i=0\), hence \(i=j\).

None of the elements in (11) is zero. If \(x^i=0\) for some \(i<M\), then
\[
 x^M=x^i x^{M-i}=0,
\]
contradicting (6), since \(1\ne0\) in \(R_p\).

As a set, \(R_p\) consists of all ordered pairs of residues modulo \(p\), so it has exactly
\(p^2\) elements. Exactly one of these is zero. The \(M\) distinct nonzero powers in (11) must therefore fit among only \(p^2-1\) nonzero elements. Hence every prime divisor \(p\) of \(N\) satisfies
\[
 M\le p^2-1,
\]
or equivalently
\[
 M+1\le p^2.                                                       \tag{12}
\]

We can now prove that \(N\) is prime. Certainly \(M>2\), so \(N=M-1>1\). Suppose for contradiction that \(N\) is composite, and let \(p\) be its least prime factor. For a composite positive integer, its least prime factor satisfies
\[
 p^2\le N.                                                         \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, writing \(N=pr\), if \(r<p\), then a prime factor of \(r\) would be a prime factor of \(N\) smaller than \(p\); therefore \(r\ge p\), and \(N=pr\ge p^2\).

On the other hand, because \(p\mid N\), (12) applies and gives
\[
 M+1\le p^2.
\]
Combining this with (13) and \(N=M-1\) yields
\[
 M+1\le p^2\le N=M-1,
\]
an impossibility. Thus \(N\) is prime.

Finally, consider the set used to define the sequence value at \(n=100943\):
\[
 S=\left\{m\in\mathbb N:
 m>0\ \text{and}\ 2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1\text{ is prime}\right\}.
\]
We have proved that
\[
 2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1=N
\]
is prime, and of course \(39101>0\). Hence \(39101\in S\), so \(S\) is nonempty. By well-ordering, its least element belongs to \(S\); in particular that least element is strictly positive. The definition of \(a(100943)\) is precisely this least element (with value \(0\) only when no such positive exponent exists). Therefore
\[
 a(100943)>0,
\]
and consequently
\[
 a(100943)\ne0.
\]
This disproves the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\).
